chapter.title: Idioms and Phrasal Verbs (The Strict Separation Rule)
chapter.description: A register-focused chapter separating informal Speaking idioms from formal Writing Task 2 collocations and phrases. It contains 50 Speaking idioms, 50 academic Writing collocations and phrases, and two practice exercises.
learning_objectives: Use informal idioms naturally in IELTS Speaking rather than Writing Task 2.
Recognise the register difference between conversational idioms and formal academic language.
Use 50 formal Task 2 collocations and phrases appropriately.
Recognise informal phrasal verbs that should be avoided in formal essays.
Correct commonly misremembered or misused idioms.

blocks.title: The Strict Separation Rule
blocks.content: This chapter rests on one rule that decides more Lexical Resource marks than any other single habit: informal idioms belong in Speaking, not in Writing Task 2. The same expression that earns you a point in the interview can cost you one in the essay. This is not a small stylistic preference; it is a register rule, and register is exactly what the higher bands test. Here is why the split is so sharp. IELTS Speaking rewards natural, spontaneous language, so a well-placed idiom (it was a blessing in disguise, I was over the moon) signals that you can use English the way a fluent speaker actually does. Writing Task 2, by contrast, is a formal academic essay. In that context an idiom reads as casual, unserious, and out of place, and it pulls your tone down toward Band 6 no matter how impressive the idiom is. The examiner is not asking “does this candidate know idioms.” The examiner is asking “does this candidate know where each kind of language belongs.” The decision rule. Before you use an expression in writing, ask: would this sound natural in a newspaper editorial or an academic article? If yes, it is safe for Task 2. If it would sound at home in a friendly chat, keep it for Speaking. Part A of this chapter gives you fifty expressions built for Speaking and fifty built for Writing, each labelled, so you can build the instinct. Never mix the two columns. A note on phrasal verbs: many are neutral and perfectly fine in writing (carry out, bring about, result in). The ones to keep out of Task 2 are the informal, idiomatic ones (get its act together, cough up, pull your socks up). When in doubt, choose the single formal verb (organise, pay, improve).

decision_rule.safe_for_task2: Would this sound natural in a newspaper editorial or an academic article?
decision_rule.keep_for_speaking: Would this sound at home in a friendly chat?

blocks.phrasal_verb_note: Many are neutral and perfectly fine in writing (carry out, bring about, result in). The informal, idiomatic ones to keep out of Task 2 are get its act together, cough up, and pull your socks up. When in doubt, choose the single formal verb (organise, pay, improve).

blocks.title: Part A1: 50 Speaking Idioms
blocks.intro: Use these to sound natural in the interview. The Part label shows where each fits best. Do not carry any of them into a Task 2 essay.

items.example: I eat out once in a blue moon.
For me, cooking is a piece of cake.

items.expression: cost an arm and a leg
items.example: Concert tickets cost an arm and a leg.
My office is a stone’s throw away from home.
That cafe is a total rip-off.
We hit it off the moment we met.

items.meaning: to stop working for the day
items.example: By six, I usually call it a day.

items.meaning: to learn how to do something
items.example: It took me a week to get the hang of it.
I often lend a hand at home.
My parents always said money doesn’t grow on trees.
I was over the moon when I passed.
On my wedding day, I was on cloud nine.
I felt down in the dumps after the result.
I had butterflies in my stomach before the interview.

items.meaning: to become nervous at the last minute
items.example: I nearly got cold feet before the speech.
On my first day abroad, I felt like a fish out of water.

items.meaning: the final thing one can tolerate
items.example: The delay was the last straw.

items.meaning: a hidden benefit in a setback
items.example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
The view was the icing on the cake.

items.meaning: thrown into something difficult with no preparation
items.example: I was thrown in at the deep end on day one.

items.meaning: to work or study late into the night
items.bangla: Before finals, I burn the midnight oil.

items.example: I need to hit the books this weekend.
Good teachers go the extra mile.
I had to pull my socks up after the mock test.
Let me get the ball rolling on the project.

items.meaning: to begin to understand or manage
items.example: It takes time to get to grips with a new city.
An internship gets your foot in the door.

items.meaning: to become independent and try new things
items.example: University lets young people spread their wings.
I learned time management the hard way.
Businesses must keep up with the times.

items.expression: hit the nail on the head
items.meaning: to say exactly the right thing
items.example: You’ve hit the nail on the head.

items.bangla: Leaders must see the bigger picture.

items.example: Innovation means thinking outside the box.

items.meaning: to stay receptive to new ideas
items.example: It helps to keep an open mind.
On this issue, I refuse to sit on the fence.

items.meaning: something with both good and bad sides
items.bangla: Social media is a mixed blessing.

items.example: Remote work offers the best of both worlds.

items.expression: every cloud has a silver lining
items.example: Every cloud has a silver lining.
My colleague and I are on the same wavelength.
During the crisis, we were all in the same boat.

items.expression: kill two birds with one stone
items.meaning: to solve two things at once
items.bangla: Cycling to work kills two birds with one stone.

items.expression: at the drop of a hat
items.example: She would travel at the drop of a hat.

items.meaning: to make a bad situation worse
items.example: His comment only added fuel to the fire.
Finding a quiet flat there is like finding a needle in a haystack.

items.meaning: to use influence to get something
items.example: He pulled strings to get the job.
Sooner or later, you have to face the music.

items.expression: bite off more than you can chew
items.bangla: I bit off more than I could chew last term.

items.example: The resort was in the middle of nowhere.
A holiday gives you a change of scenery.
Visiting the mountains was the trip of a lifetime.

blocks.title: Part A2: 50 Academic Writing Collocations and Phrases
blocks.intro: Use these in Writing Task 2. Every one is formal and essay-appropriate.

items.example: It is widely acknowledged that education reduces poverty.
There is no denying that technology has reshaped work.

items.expression: a growing body of evidence suggests that
items.example: A growing body of evidence suggests that pollution harms cognition.
It can be argued that fees limit access.

items.expression: this essay will examine both views
items.example: This essay will examine both views before offering an opinion.
A widely held view is that competition improves standards.
It stands to reason that better roads reduce delays.
There is a compelling argument for renewable subsidies.
Opponents make a valid point about cost.
Proponents argue that automation raises productivity.
Critics contend that it destroys jobs.
It is worth noting that results vary by region.

items.bangla: Education plays a pivotal role in development.

items.example: Rapid growth gives rise to inequality.
Many problems stem from poverty.
The decline can be attributed to weak demand.
Poor diet is a contributing factor in obesity.
As a direct result of the ban, sales fell.
While it is true that costs are high, benefits outweigh them.

items.bangla: Contrary to popular belief, remote work can raise output.
Despite the fact that it is costly, the plan is justified.

items.expression: on the one hand … on the other hand
items.example: On the one hand it saves time; on the other, it isolates people.
This is true to a certain extent.
Governments must address the issue urgently.

items.meaning: to deal with the underlying reason
items.bangla: Lasting change means tackling the root cause.

items.meaning: to put good policies in place
items.example: Cities should implement effective measures against pollution.
Public transport is a viable solution to congestion.

items.bangla: Policymakers must weigh the pros and cons.

items.example: We must strike a balance between growth and conservation.
Any policy must take into account rural needs.
A significant proportion of graduates work abroad.
The vast majority of commuters use trains.
In the long run, prevention is cheaper.
In the short term, costs may rise.
Art is an integral part of education.
The movement has gained momentum.
Rising seas pose a serious threat to coasts.
Stress has a detrimental effect on health.
Future generations will reap the benefits of this investment.
Growth should not come at the expense of the environment.
Singapore is a case in point.
To illustrate this, consider public transport in Tokyo.
We must bear in mind that resources are finite.
The study sheds light on the causes.
In light of these findings, reform is needed.
From my perspective, the benefits outweigh the risks.
More often than not, early action is cheaper.
By and large, the policy has succeeded.
It is difficult to draw a firm conclusion from limited data.

blocks.title: Exercise 5.1 · Register and Style Sort
blocks.instructions: Each sentence below is written as if it appeared in a Writing Task 2 essay. Decide whether the underlined language is appropriate for a formal essay (mark it W) or belongs only in Speaking (mark it S). For every S, rewrite the sentence in formal academic English suitable for Task 2.

questions.prompt: Nowadays, a lot of kids are glued to their phones around the clock.
It is widely acknowledged that education reduces poverty.
The government needs to get its act together on pollution.
This policy could have far-reaching consequences.
At the end of the day, it is up to the individual.
Renewable energy plays a pivotal role in cutting emissions.
Fast food is a rip-off and bad for you.
There is no denying that technology has transformed education.
Loads of people reckon that exams are unfair.
Poverty can be attributed to a range of social factors.
Young people these days could not care less about tradition.
Governments must strike a balance between growth and conservation.
Social media is a double-edged sword, to be honest.
This crisis stems from decades of underinvestment.
If you ask me, the whole system is a mess.
A growing body of evidence suggests a link between diet and disease.
Tourism can boost the economy, but it is a bit of a mixed bag.
In the long run, prevention is cheaper than treatment.
The rich should cough up more tax.
It is worth noting that not all solutions are equally effective.

blocks.title: Exercise 5.2 · Idiom Substitution
blocks.instructions: Each Speaking response below contains an idiom that is misremembered, misused, or wrong. Rewrite the underlined part with the correct, natural form.

questions.prompt: When I got the scholarship, I was on cloud seven.
The final test was a piece of pie for me.
On my first day abroad, I felt like a fish in the water.
My university is just a stone throw from my house.
Learning to drive was a really steep hill at first.
We managed to kill two birds in one stone by cycling to work.
After the experiment failed, it was back to the painting board.
Honestly, I would travel at the drop of the hat. End of Chapter 5. Chapter 6, the Full Workbook and Self-Assessment, follows.

Part A1: 50 Speaking Idioms

Part A2: 50 Academic Writing Collocations and Phrases
Use these in Writing Task 2. Every one is formal and essay-appropriate.
Introducing and framing
1.
it is widely acknowledged that: many accept as true. Bangla: 
 
 
 “
ব্যাপকভাবেস্বীকৃতযে।
It is 
widely acknowledged that education reduces poverty.”
2.
there is no denying that: it cannot be denied. Bangla: 
 
 
 
 
 “
অস্বীকারকরারউপায়নেইযে।
There 
is no denying that technology has reshaped work.”
3.
a growing body of evidence suggests that: increasing research indicates. Bangla: 
 
 
 
 
 “
ক্রমবর্ধমানপ্রমাণণইঙ্গিতকরেযে।
A growing body of evidence suggests that pollution harms 
cognition.”
4.
it can be argued that: one could reasonably claim. Bangla: 
 
 
 
 
 “
যুক্তিদেওয়াযেতে
পারেযে।
It 
can be argued that fees limit access.”

5.

এইরচনায়উভয়মত 
 
 
 “

This essay will examine both views before offering an opinion.”
6.

 “
ব্যাপকভাবেপ্রচলিতমত।

view is that competition improves standards.”

 “
এটাযুক্তিসঙ্গতযে।
It stands to reason 
that better roads reduce delays.”
8.

 “
জোরালো
যুক্তি।
There is a 
compelling argument for renewable subsidies.”
9.

 “
যুক্তিসংগতবক্তব্য।
Opponents make a valid 
point about cost.”

 “

 “

 “
